chapter: With King Oliver in New York
title: Drumming for early recording: padded bass drum, mallets, microphones
summary: Moore describes muting the bass drum with quilts, using soft mallets on cymbals, sitting close to the microphone, and playing softly with wood blocks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah, I played it for, uh, Paul Barber one time. But during that time, when he recorded, you kept your bass drum padded. Mm-hmm. You put quilts and all, everything in front of the bass. You didn't want to hear no bass drum. All you want to hear that snare drum, snare so down low, like a tom-tom effect, not quite a tom-tom effect. Mm-hmm. And when you hit the cymbal, you don't hit it with the sticks. You use a soft mallet. Mm-hmm. You hit the cymbal and choke it. Cut it off.
You make the needle jump on the record some days.

Yeah. You couldn't use the sticks and pound on them like it, you know. You couldn't. Where would they make you sit, a drummer? Would he be in close to the microphone or far from it or what? Close to the mic. Pretty close. Yeah, pretty close. I had a mic hanging right over.
But they'd have old pillars and quilts and things. In the front of the drum, keep it in the middle. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. recording through those long horns. What you call them things? Yeah, the microphone. Didn't have it set up that they got now, you know, the different things.
Well, how would that change your style to record? What would you do different?
You wouldn't stand playing somewhat softer on it.
You wouldn't change your style. You just play soft and use your mallets.
Could you use your wood blocks, for example? Oh yeah, your wood blocks.
